title: Rahula's mirror for children
hookLine: a broken flowerpot, two grown-ups, and the mirror the Buddha gave his son (MN 61)
tomorrow: why would a monk stay hidden in a field all night?

lines: WHAT DID YOU THINK WOULD HAPPEN?
cards: A ball, a porch, a flowerpot in pieces, and a small kid frozen in place. Two grown-ups walk up. The first says: we have a rule about balls near the porch, and rules are rules.
The second crouches down: what did you think would happen when you kicked it there? The kid looks from one face to the other, waiting to see which one wins. Both grown-ups love this kid.
Both are trying to guide, and neither is wrong to try. Inside the Buddhist world, both answers have a long life too.

teach.b: The second voice has a well-known source. The Buddha's son, Rahula, was young and living among the monks. The Buddha takes a water dipper with a little water left in it and asks: do you see how little is left?
That's how little there is to the training of someone who lies on purpose without shame. Then he picks up a mirror.
What's a mirror for, Rahula? For looking at yourself.
So, before you act, while you act, and after, look: will this harm me, or someone else, or both? If it will, don't do it. If it did, own it to someone wise, and learn.
Here's the first voice, at its best. A child can't weigh everything yet. Clear lines are a gift: don't hit, don't take, don't lie.

The precepts are part of the path from the start, and novices take them on, so the questions have firm ground to stand on. A rule holds on the days reflection is too slow. Now the second voice, at its best.
A rule kept only because someone's watching breaks when they leave.

A child who learns to ask what might happen carries the teacher inside. Notice the sutta itself: it opens with a firm line about lying, then hands over the mirror. Teachers today weigh the two differently.

how: Some Buddhist parents and Sunday-school teachers use Rahula's mirror with children, asking what might happen before they act; children and novices also learn the precepts.

games.q: what does “rahula's mirror for children” mean?
o: a rule that children must confess every mistake to a monk
a reward a child gets for keeping all the precepts
looking at an action before, during and after: who might it harm?

games.q: the mirror lesson — tap the pairs.
p: how little is left for a liar
will this harm me, or others, or both?

s: in the sutta, the Buddha gives Rahula only questions, never a firm line
it opens with a firm line about deliberate lying, then hands over the mirror.
the mirror is used after acting as well as before
before, during and after; if harm was done, own it to someone wise.

games.q: your aunt says kids need clear rules first; your friend says rules make kids sneaky and only questions work. state your aunt's best case.
o: rules are easier for adults, so they're simply better for everyone.
a child can't weigh everything yet; firm lines hold on the days reflection is too slow.
questions are pointless for kids, since children can't really think about harm.
games.why: that's the rule side at its best, and the sutta itself starts with a firm line before the mirror. teachers still weigh the two differently.

practice: Bring up something you'll do in the next hour: a message, a meal, a conversation. Hold the mirror up to it before it happens. Ask, quietly, the way you might ask a child: what might happen, and could it harm me or someone else?
If something shifts, let it, then let the question rest, and just breathe with whatever answer comes.

wordCard.voice: Rahula's mirror for children: look before, during and after; ask who it might harm. A question a child can carry.

orig.note: Pali: a mirror, the object the Buddha holds up for Rahula.

carryVoice: Keep this one close: reflect first, then act, and look again after. Nine of eleven on family.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 61 (Ambalatthika Rahulovada Sutta: the water dipper and deliberate lying; the mirror; reflecting before, during and after deeds of body, speech and mind; confessing harmful deeds to the Teacher or wise companions)
